summary: This informational RFC defines S/MIME Capability types, encoded in ASN.1, for the public key types defined by the PKIX working group. A requester can then say which public keys and signature algorithms it wants in responses.

plainLanguage.summary: Before sending a coded letter, you can say which kinds of code you can read. This gives names for those key types.

questions: what are s/mime capabilities for public keys
how to specify pkix key types in s/mime
how to specify rsa key sizes in s/mime
how to declare elliptic curve support
subtitle: ASN.1 definitions for declaring support for public key algorithms and sizes.

tldr.problem: When sending encrypted mail or requesting certificates, the sender needs to tell the recipient which public key types and sizes it can handle, but no standard way existed to specify public key preferences.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC defines S/MIME Capability types (encoded in ASN.1) for all the major public key types—RSA, DSA, Diffie-Hellman, and Elliptic Curve—allowing the sender to advertise minimum and maximum key sizes, specific curves, or restricted algorithm use.
tldr.outcome: Senders and receivers can negotiate which key types and sizes to use in cryptographic exchanges without guessing or falling back to weak algorithms.

today: RFC 6664 is an Informational document that defines how to express public key preferences in S/MIME capabilities. It remains current for OCSP and certificate request exchanges where key type negotiation is needed.

sections.title: S/MIME Capabilities and Public Keys
sections.content: S/MIME (Secure/Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions) lets mail users send encrypted and signed messages. S/MIME capabilities are fields in a message that tell the recipient which encryption and signature algorithms the sender supports. Historically, S/MIME capabilities covered encryption algorithms like AES and 3DES, but they did not cover public key types. This document fills that gap by defining capability types for the public keys used in the PKIX (Public Key Infrastructure X.509) standard. With these capabilities, a sender can specify that it wants an RSA key of at least 2048 bits, or an Elliptic Curve key on a specific curve, enabling proper algorithm negotiation in certificate requests and secure mail exchanges.
sections.plainLanguage: When asking for a new lock, you can say: 'Give me an RSA lock with at least 2048 bits,' and you are both on the same page.

sections.title: How Capabilities Work
sections.content: S/MIME capabilities are part of a message or certificate and form a list of algorithm identifiers with optional parameters. Each capability specifies an Object Identifier (OID), a code that uniquely identifies the algorithm, and an optional parameters field. The parameters field allows fine-grained control: for example, specifying that only a certain range of RSA key sizes is acceptable. The capabilities are encoded in ASN.1, a standard notation for structured data. A sender publishes its list in order of preference, and the recipient picks the first algorithm in the list that it also supports. A critical principle is that the capabilities should be specific enough that the recipient does not have to guess which combinations are supported. If you list RSA, EC-DSA, SHA-1, and SHA-256, the recipient might assume you support all four combinations (RSA with SHA-1, RSA with SHA-256, EC-DSA with SHA-1, EC-DSA with SHA-256), which may not be true.
sections.plainLanguage: You list the locks you like in order. The other person picks the first one they also have. You should be clear about which combinations work together.

sections.title: RSA Public Keys and Sizes
sections.content: There are three RSA public key types in PKIX. The generic RSA key (rsaEncryption) can be used for both encryption and signature verification, and is the most common in certificates. The S/MIME capability for generic RSA lets the sender specify minimum and optional maximum key sizes in bits. For example, a sender might advertise support for RSA keys of at least 2048 bits and at most 4096 bits. The RFC recommends certain common sizes: 1024, 2048, 3072, 4096, 7680, 8192, and 15360 bits (the larger values follow NIST guidance), but other sizes can be used. The second RSA type is RSASSA-PSS, a signature algorithm that the sender can use if it wants to restrict a key to signing only. The third is RSAES-OAEP, a key encryption algorithm that restricts a key to encryption only. Both RSASSA-PSS and RSAES-OAEP use the same capability format as generic RSA—minimum and optional maximum sizes.
sections.plainLanguage: For RSA locks, you can say: 'I want at least 2048 bits.' You can also say you only want it for signing, or only for encrypting.

sections.title: Diffie-Hellman and Elliptic Curve Keys
sections.content: Diffie-Hellman (DH) keys are used for key agreement (not signing). There are two DH types: DSA (used for digital signatures) and DH key agreement. Both use similar capability formats. For DH keys, the sender can specify minimum and optional maximum key sizes, plus optional maximum sizes for the key's mathematical components (p, q, and g). Alternatively, the sender can specify exact DH parameters to be used. Elliptic Curve (ECC) keys are popular for modern cryptography because they offer strong security with smaller key sizes. There are three ECC types: generic EC (for both agreement and signature), EC-DH (for key agreement only), and EC-MQV (a variant of EC-DH). For ECC, the sender specifies which curves it supports rather than key sizes, because choosing the right curve is more nuanced than choosing a key size. The sender lists one or more named curves (such as P-256, P-384, P-521) to indicate which curves are acceptable.
sections.plainLanguage: For Diffie-Hellman locks, you say the minimum bits you want. For Elliptic Curve, you name which curves work for you.

sections.title: RSASSA-PSS Signature Algorithm Capability
sections.content: RSASSA-PSS is a probabilistic signature algorithm that combines RSA with cryptographic hashing and masking. The standard capability format for RSASSA-PSS was defined in RFC 4055, but that format only specified the OID without parameters. When a sender publishes an S/MIME capability for RSASSA-PSS signatures, it now needs to say which hash algorithms and masking algorithms it supports alongside the signature algorithm. This RFC defines a new capability type for RSASSA-PSS that includes both the hash algorithm and the masking algorithm as parameters. A hash algorithm field specifies which hash function (such as SHA-1, SHA-256, SHA-384) the sender will use. A mask algorithm field specifies the masking function (typically MGF1, a mask generation function). A trailer field parameter specifies the RSASSA-PSS trailer (always the value 1). This bundling of hash, mask, and trailer in one capability prevents mismatched combinations: the recipient knows that if you advertise an RSASSA-PSS capability with SHA-256 and MGF1, you will actually use that combination.
sections.plainLanguage: When signing with RSASSA-PSS, you say which hash and mask you use together in one package, so there is no confusion.
